claim: Translesion DNA polymerase kappa (PolK) is required for efficient replication fork restart after hydroxyurea (HU) treatment.
source: Unexpectedly, only PolK, but not Polζ, or other members of the Y-family TLS Pols, is required to promote efficient fork restart after HU treatment, as shown by the increased percentage of stalled forks (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber analysis showing increased stalled forks when PolK is depleted, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PolK-mediated fork restart is dependent on the duration of HU treatment, being effective within 4 hours but not at 8 hours or longer.
source: This appears to be the case as the ability of PolK to rescue stalled forks is linked to a shorter duration of HU treatment (within 4 hr) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C). In contrast, if replication forks are stalled for too long (8 hr or greater), the number of stalled forks increases dramatically even in control cells and they become less dependent on a PolK for fork restart.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data comparing different HU treatment durations shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Supplementing media with deoxynucleosides (dNs) in the presence of HU can rescue stalled forks to the same level as washing out HU.
source: We found that the percentage of stalled forks were very similar when comparing samples with normal fork restart after HU wash off versus samples with added dNs under continuous HU treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data comparing fork restart with HU wash off versus dN supplementation, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rescue of stalled forks by deoxynucleoside supplementation correlates with checkpoint recovery as measured by decreased phosphorylated Chk1 and RPA32.
source: The rescue of stalled forks in the presence of high-dose HU correlated with checkpoint recovery (decrease in phosphorylated Ser345 Chk1 and Ser33 RPA32 signals) after supplementing with dNs, but not with ribonucleosides (rNs) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing changes in phosphorylated checkpoint proteins after dN supplementation, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HU primarily acts as a potent inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase (RNR), preventing conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides.
source: This is consistent with the fact that HU primarily acts as a potent inhibitor of RNR, which prevents the conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, leading to nucleotide deprivation and fork stalling.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about HU's mechanism of action.

claim: Aphidicolin (APH) treatment results in higher levels of fork stalling compared to HU treatment in control samples.
source: Interestingly, in control samples, APH treatment followed by a wash off resulted in higher levels of fork-stalling in comparison to HU treatment, and the depletion of PolK did not further increase fork-stalling events (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data comparing HU and APH treatments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Depletion of PolK does not further increase fork stalling after APH treatment.
source: Interestingly, in control samples, APH treatment followed by a wash off resulted in higher levels of fork-stalling in comparison to HU treatment, and the depletion of PolK did not further increase fork-stalling events (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Stalled fork structures in HU-treated cells are processed differently than in APH-treated cells.
source: We speculate that the stalled fork structures in HU- versus APH-treated cells are likely processed differently (Vesela et al., 2017; Barlow et al., 2013) due to the fact that unlike HU, APH treatment does not lead to RPA phosphorylation even though both can activate Chk1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by Western blot data in Figure 1F and citations to previous literature.

claim: APH is a reversible, potent and specific inhibitor of B-family DNA polymerases including Polα, Polδ, and Polε.
source: APH is a reversible, potent and specific inhibitor of B-family DNA polymerases (Vesela et al., 2017), which includes Polα and the replicative DNA polymerasesδ and ε.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Vesela et al., 2017).

claim: Unlike HU, APH treatment does not lead to RPA phosphorylation even though both can activate Chk1.
source: We speculate that the stalled fork structures in HU- versus APH-treated cells are likely processed differently (Vesela et al., 2017; Barlow et al., 2013) due to the fact that unlike HU, APH treatment does not lead to RPA phosphorylation even though both can activate Chk1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Gemcitabine (Gem) acts as a nucleoside analog that blocks DNA synthesis.
source: Gem, on the other hand, acts as a nucleoside analog that blocks DNA synthesis (Mini et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Mini et al., 2006).

claim: Fork restart was not detected after washing off Gemcitabine at various doses.
source: Under our conditions, we failed to detect fork restart and checkpoint recovery after washing off Gem at various doses, thus precluding any analysis of fork restart (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: FANCD2-deficient patient cells (PD20) show defective fork restart that can be corrected by FANCD2 WT complementation but not by the monoubiquitination-defective K561R mutant.
source: In an extension of our previous findings (Chen et al., 2015), FA fibroblasts from FANCD2-deficient patient cells (PD20) showed defective fork restart that could be corrected by FANCD2 WT complementation, but not its monoubiquitination-defective mutant K561R (Garcia-Higuera et al., 2001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous work.

claim: Additional knockdown of PolK in FANCD2-deficient cells does not further increase the level of stalled forks, suggesting PolK is epistatic to the FA pathway for fork restart.
source: However, the additional knockdown of PolK in PD20 vector control or K561R mutant-expressing cells did not further increase the level of stalled forks, suggesting that PolK is likely epistatic to the FA pathway to facilitate fork restart (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GFP-tagged PolK wild-type expression can rescue defective fork restart in PolK CRISPR cells, but is incapable of rescue when FANCD2 is simultaneously depleted.
source: Importantly, the analysis of one of the 293T PolK CRISPR clones (sgPolK #1) demonstrated that GFP-tagged PolK wild-type (WT) expression can rescue defective fork restart, but is incapable of rescue when FANCD2 is simultaneously depleted by siRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ability of PolK to promote fork restart correlates with longer track lengths of DNA synthesis after HU wash off.
source: The ability of PolK to promote fork restart also strongly correlated with longer track lengths of DNA synthesis after HU wash off (quantifying the length of the red tracks only in fork events containing both green and red tracks) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber tract length measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PolK-mediated fork restart requires the activation of the FA pathway.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that PolK-mediated fork restart requires the activation of the FA pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing epistasis between PolK and FANCD2.

claim: ATR-dependent Chk1 phosphorylation on Ser345 is unaffected by the loss of PolK or FANCD2 in response to HU treatment.
source: Surprisingly, using our experimental setting, both ATR-dependent Chk1 phosphorylation on Ser345 or RPA32 phosphorylation on Ser33 (or Ser4/8) were unaffected by the loss of PolK or FANCD2 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) in different cell lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RPA32 phosphorylation on Ser33 (or Ser4/8) is unaffected by the loss of PolK or FANCD2 in response to HU treatment.
source: Surprisingly, using our experimental setting, both ATR-dependent Chk1 phosphorylation on Ser345 or RPA32 phosphorylation on Ser33 (or Ser4/8) were unaffected by the loss of PolK or FANCD2 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) in different cell lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reconstitution of GFP-PolK WT in PolK CRISPR cells does not alter the kinetics of checkpoint recovery of phosphorylated Chk1 or RPA after HU wash off.
source: Even in the 293T PolK CRISPR clone (sgPolK clone #1), the reconstitution of GFP-PolK WT did not alter the kinetics of checkpoint recovery of phosphorylated Chk1 or RPA after HU wash off (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The levels of PCNA monoubiquitination are higher in GFP-PolK WT-expressing cells compared to vector control cells in response to HU treatment.
source: However, the levels of PCNA monoubiquitination (mUb-PCNA) was higher in the GFP-PolK WT-expressing sgPolK clone #1 293 T cells in comparison to the vector control cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PolK has been previously shown to directly interact with monoubiquitinated PCNA.
source: As PolK has been previously shown to directly interact with mUb-PCNA (Jones et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2008), this suggests that expression of PolK may help stabilize mUb-PCNA in response to HU treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Jones et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2008).

claim: Expression of PolK may help stabilize monoubiquitinated PCNA in response to HU treatment.
source: As PolK has been previously shown to directly interact with mUb-PCNA (Jones et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2008), this suggests that expression of PolK may help stabilize mUb-PCNA in response to HU treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from Western blot data and previous literature.

claim: GFP-tagged PolK WT, but not the UBZ mutant, interacts with monoubiquitinated PCNA in an HU-dependent manner.
source: We found that GFP-tagged PolK WT, but not mutations of both UBDs (UBZ mutant), was able to interact with mUb-PCNA in an HU-dependent manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by crosslinking immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interaction of PolK with FANCD2, FANCI, RPA, or unmodified PCNA is not HU-inducible and not dependent on its ubiquitin-binding domains.
source: However, the interaction of PolK with FANCD2, FANCI, RPA, or even unmodified PCNA, was not HU-inducible, nor was it dependent on its UBDs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by crosslinking immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PolK interacts with differentially polyubiquitinated forms of PCNA (di- or tri-ubiquitinated) in HU-treated cells.
source: The detection of additional higher molecular weight mUb-PCNA antibody-reactive bands in the anti-GFP antibody pull-down assay suggests that PolK is likely interacting with differentially polyubiquitinated (di- or tri-ubiquitinated) forms of PCNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from Western blot data showing higher molecular weight PCNA bands in Figure 3C.

claim: HU-induced polyubiquitinated PCNA contains K48-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Surprisingly, when using a purified SARS-PLpro deubiquitinating (DUB) enzyme that exclusively cleaves longer K48-linked ubiquitin chains (but not monoubiquitinated substrates) (Békés et al., 2016; Békés et al., 2015), the higher molecular weight species of PCNA (likely di- or triUb-PCNA) were greatly reduced when incubated with PLpro WT, but not its catalytic mutant (C112A) or the AMSH K63 chain cleavage-specific metalloprotease (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitin chain restriction analysis data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, along with citations to previous work on DUB specificity.

claim: PolK mostly interacts with K48-linked polyubiquitinated PCNA in HU-treated cells.
source: Using this in vitro ubiquitin chain restriction analysis, it supports the notion that PolK mostly interacts with K48-linked polyubiquitinated PCNA in HU-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ubiquitin chain restriction analysis data.

claim: The ubiquitin-binding capacity of PolK is required for PolK-mediated fork restart.
source: Using the CRISPR sgPolK cells that are transiently transfected with either GFP-tagged PolK WT or the UBZ mutant, we showed that the ubiquitin-binding capacity of PolK is required for PolK-mediated fork restart (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The catalytically dead mutant of PolK is unable to properly perform fork restart.
source: Importantly, the catalytically dead (CD) mutant of PolK (DE198/199AA) was also unable to properly perform fork restart.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both the DNA polymerase activity and ubiquitin-mediated transactions are essential for PolK-dependent recovery of stalled replication forks.
source: This demonstrates that both the DNA polymerase activity and ubiquitin-mediated transactions (likely through polyubiquitinated PCNA) are essential for PolK-dependent recovery of stalled replication forks (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from DNA fiber analysis data showing both CD and UBZ mutants fail to rescue fork restart.

claim: The ubiquitination mutant (K164R) of PCNA has compromised fork restart after HU treatment.
source: In line with the requirement of the UBDs of PolK for proper fork restart, we also showed that the ubiquitination mutant (K164R) of PCNA has compromised fork restart after HU treatment (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The FA pathway and other HDR proteins such as Rad51 and BRCA2 are required for fork protection against nascent DNA degradation.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Schlacher et al., 2012; Schlacher et al., 2011; Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016), we showed that FANCD2 and other HDR-related factors, Rad51 and BRCA2, are required for fork protection (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures, along with citations to previous literature.

claim: Rad51 and BRCA2 are not required for efficient fork restart.
source: However, in contrast to FANCD2, both Rad51 and BRCA2 are not required for efficient fork restart (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mechanisms involving HDR to prevent fork collapse are separable from fork restart under the HU treatment conditions used.
source: This suggests that mechanisms involving HDR to prevent fork collapse, such as fork reversals, are separable from fork restart as defined by our HU treatment conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Rad51 and BRCA2 are required for fork protection but not fork restart.

claim: PolK depletion causes a reduction in nascent DNA tract length, indicating a role in fork protection.
source: Similar to a FANCD2 loss, we found that PolK depletion caused a reduction in the nascent DNA tract length (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Expression of GFP-PolK WT in CRISPR sgPolK cells can reverse nascent DNA degradation in HU-treated cells.
source: Additionally, expression of GFP-PolK WT back into the CRISPR sgPolK cells can reverse nascent DNA degradation in HU-treated cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The catalytically dead mutant of PolK can partially rescue nascent DNA degradation, but the UBZ mutant cannot.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the CD mutant, but not the UBZ mutant of PolK, can still partially rescue PolK deficiency in preventing nascent DNA degradation (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The polymerase activity is not as critical for preventing nascent DNA degradation as it is for mediating fork restart efficiency.
source: This argues that the polymerase activity is not as critical for preventing nascent DNA degradation as it is for mediating fork restart efficiency, thus revealing a possible mechanistic difference between PolK's role in fork restart versus fork protection.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential rescue abilities of CD and UBZ mutants in fork protection versus fork restart assays.

claim: MRE11 nuclease is critical for nascent DNA degradation of stalled replication forks in FA pathway- or BRCA2-deficient cells.
source: The MRE11 nuclease was previously shown to be critical for nascent DNA degradation of stalled replication forks in FA pathway- or BRCA2-deficient cells (Schlacher et al., 2012; Schlacher et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Schlacher et al., 2012; Schlacher et al., 2011).

claim: SMARCAL1 acts upstream of MRE11 and is responsible for processing stalled forks to the reversed fork structure, enabling MRE11-dependent nucleolytic degradation.
source: Recent data also suggests that the SNF2-family of fork remodelers, such as SMARCAL1, acts upstream of MRE11 and is responsible for the processing of stalled forks to the reversed fork structure, enabling MRE11-dependent nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA (Taglialatela et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Taglialatela et al., 2017).

claim: Both mirin treatment and SMARCAL1 knockdown reverse nascent DNA degradation in HU-treated PolK-deficient cells.
source: Both mirin treatment and SMARCAL1 knockdown reversed the nascent DNA degradation observed in HU-treated PolK-deficient cells (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: Inhibition of MRE11 activity or SMARCAL1 depletion has no effect on fork restart after HU treatment.
source: Remarkably, inhibition of either MRE11 activity or SMARCAL1 had no effect on fork restart after HU treatment (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 4D and 4F.

claim: PolK rescues stalled forks via two non-overlapping mechanisms: fork protection against SMARCAL1- and MRE11-dependent nucleolytic degradation, and replication fork restart.
source: This implies that PolK is capable of rescuing stalled forks via two non-overlapping mechanisms: 1) fork protection against SMARCAL1- and MRE11-dependent nucleolytic degradation, and 2) replication fork restart.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing that rescuing fork protection does not affect fork restart defects.

claim: The tract length is slightly elevated (faster fork speed) in the absence of PolK in untreated cells.
source: Indeed, by DNA fiber analysis, we show that the tract length is slightly elevated (faster fork speed) in the absence of PolK, while USP1 knockdown can lead to a PolK-dependent slow-down of the replication fork in the absence of HU treatment, as demonstrated in our previous study (Jones et al., 2012) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citation to previous work.

claim: USP1 knockdown leads to a PolK-dependent slow-down of the replication fork in the absence of HU treatment.
source: Indeed, by DNA fiber analysis, we show that the tract length is slightly elevated (faster fork speed) in the absence of PolK, while USP1 knockdown can lead to a PolK-dependent slow-down of the replication fork in the absence of HU treatment, as demonstrated in our previous study (Jones et al., 2012) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citation to previous work (Jones et al., 2012).

claim: Aberrant recruitment of PolK to the replication fork can lead to reduced DNA synthesis and genomic instability in unperturbed dividing cells.
source: Thus, in unperturbed, dividing cells, the aberrant recruitment of PolK to the replication fork can lead to reduced DNA synthesis and genomic instability (Jones et al., 2012; Mansilla et al., 2016), which is likely due, in part, to the slowing of the normal fork speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Jones et al., 2012; Mansilla et al., 2016).

claim: Y-family DNA polymerases have the potential to operate efficiently at low dNTP concentrations compared to replicative DNA polymerases due to intrinsic differences in Km values for dNTPs.
source: For instance, in bacteria, Y-family DNA Pols have the potential to operate efficiently at low dNTP concentrations in comparison to the replicative DNA Pols due to intrinsic differences in Km values for dNTPs (Godoy et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Godoy et al., 2006) on bacterial polymerases.

claim: PolK depletion reduces DNA synthesis (fork speed) during HU treatment.
source: We found that PolK depletion further reduced DNA synthesis (or fork speed) during HU treatment, as measured by reduced CldU tract length adjacent to IdU tracts (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both PolK and FANCD2 are significantly enriched in the replisome of HU-treated cells as measured by iPOND.
source: After click chemistry with biotin, followed by streptavidin beads pull-down, we showed that both PolK and FANCD2 were significantly enriched in the replisome of HU-treated samples, but not present in thymidine-chased samples (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by iPOND experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of PolK WT, but not the CD or UBZ mutant, promotes DNA synthesis during HU treatment as measured by EdU incorporation.
source: In CRISPR sgPolK U2OS cells, the expression of PolK WT, but not the CD or UBZ mutant, promoted DNA synthesis during HU treatment (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation intensity measurements shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Expression of other Y-family TLS polymerases (Pol eta or iota) cannot compensate for reduced DNA synthesis in PolK-deficient cells under HU treatment.
source: This was not due to the over-compensation of any TLS Pols as expression of other Y-family TLS Pols, such as Pol eta or iota, could not compensate for the reduced DNA synthesis in PolK-deficient cells under HU treatment (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Among different TLS polymerases in mammalian cells, PolK possesses a unique role in facilitating DNA synthesis under conditions of nucleotide starvation.
source: Thus, amongst the different TLS Pols in mammalian cells, PolK possesses a unique role in facilitating DNA synthesis under conditions of nucleotide starvation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing only PolK, not other TLS Pols, can promote DNA synthesis under HU.

claim: The total number of EdU foci and the amount of EdU counts per foci are both reduced in PolK-depleted cells under HU treatment.
source: Using a labeling scheme to measure HU synthesis (1 hr pretreatment with 2 mM HU, followed by the addition of 10 μM EdU to HU medium), we observed that the total number of foci and the amount of EdU counts per foci are both reduced in PolK-depleted cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule localization imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PolK maintains the total number of active forks per nucleus that can synthesize under low nucleotide conditions.
source: This suggests that PolK has a role in maintaining the total number of active forks per nucleus that is able to synthesize under low nucleotide conditions, in addition to a reduction of synthesis at individual forks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from single-molecule localization imaging data showing reduced EdU foci in PolK-depleted cells.

claim: The number of EdU foci per nucleus reduced in PolK-depleted cells can be rescued when FANCD2 is depleted concomitantly.
source: While the number of EdU foci per nucleus is reduced in PolK-depleted cells, this could be rescued when FANCD2 was depleted concomitantly (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule localization imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the absence of PolK, the loss of FANCD2 may enable additional forks to undergo DNA synthesis in the presence of HU.
source: This suggests that in the absence of PolK, the loss of FANCD2 may enable additional forks (more EdU foci per nucleus) to undergo DNA synthesis in the presence of HU.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from single-molecule localization imaging data.

claim: FANCD2 may behave as a general restriction factor against aberrant DNA synthesis in response to replication stress.
source: Thus, FANCD2 may behave as a general restriction factor against aberrant DNA synthesis in response to replication stress.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the observation that FANCD2 loss rescues EdU foci numbers in PolK-deficient cells.

claim: The EdU counts per foci remain decreased in the absence of PolK, irrespective of FANCD2 levels.
source: However, the EdU counts per foci (EdU molecule intensity of individual foci) remains decreased in the absence of PolK, irrespective of FANCD2 levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule localization imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The EdU foci counts per nuclei generated by PolK is dependent on its catalytic activity.
source: Neverthless, the EdU foci counts per nuclei that is generated by PolK is still dependent on its catalytic activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule localization imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The defect in fork restart efficiency in PolK- or FANCD2-depleted cells occurs during the transition from normal elongating forks to slower-moving forks under HU treatment.
source: In summary, the defect in fork restart efficiency in either PolK- or FANCD2-depleted cells occurs at a much earlier point during the transition from normal elongating forks in untreated cells into slower-moving forks under HU treatment (Figure 5F, see working model in Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: Greater than 95% of slow-moving forks during HU treatment are converted to fast-moving restarted forks once HU is removed, irrespective of PolK or FANCD2 deficiency.
source: Surprisingly, greater than 95% of the slow-moving forks (pretreated with HU, followed by labeling with IdU for a 4 hr HU treatment) were converted to fast-moving restarted forks (labeled by CldU after HU wash off) irrespective of PolK or FANCD2 deficiency (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Forks that are competent to undergo DNA synthesis under HU independently of PolK are fully proficient to resume normal DNA synthesis once HU is removed.
source: Even though less forks are able to resume progression (restart) after pulsing with HU in either PolK- or FANCD2-deficient cells, the remaining forks that are competent to undergo DNA synthesis under HU independently of PolK, appears to be fully proficient to resume normal DNA synthesis once HU is removed.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: PolK-depleted cells show a prolonged S-phase and reduced G2 phase after a short-term HU pulse treatment.
source: Using EdU pulse-chase cell cycle analysis to directly visualize the progression of a fluorescently labeled S-phase population into the next cell cycle phase, we observed a prolonged S-phase and a reduced G2 phase in PolK-deficient cells in comparison to control cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PolK-depleted cells develop elevated senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity after short-term HU treatment followed by a 24 hr chase.
source: PolK-depleted cells also developed elevated senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-βgal) activity after a short-term HU treatment, followed by a 24 hr chase (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Depletion of p53 reverses both cell cycle delay and SA-βgal activity in PolK-deficient cells.
source: Importantly, depletion of p53 was capable of reversing both cell cycle delay (data not shown) and SA-βgal activity in PolK-deficient cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Elevated levels of 53BP1 nuclear bodies in G1 phase cells are observed in PolK-deficient cells after short-term HU treatment followed by an 18 hr chase.
source: Elevated levels of 53BP1 nuclear bodies in G1 phase cells (Cyclin A-negative) were also observed in PolK-deficient cells after a short-term HU treatment, followed by an 18 hr chase (Figure 6C), suggesting that the cause of cell cycle defects is likely due to the gradual accumulation of replication-associated DNA damage that become shielded within 53BP1 nuclear bodies for repair in the next G1 phase (Lukas et al., 2011; Harrigan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and citations to previous literature.

claim: The replication-induced DNA damage phenotype in PolK-deficient cells is comparable to that in FANCD2-depleted cells.
source: The replication-induced DNA damage phenotype shown in PolK-deficient cells is comparable to those experienced in FANCD2-depleted cells (Ceccaldi et al., 2012) (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 6A-C and citation to previous literature (Ceccaldi et al., 2012).

claim: siRNA depletion of both PolK and FANCD2 simultaneously yields similar levels of elevated SA-βgal activity and 53BP1 nuclear bodies as either individual siRNA depletion.
source: Importantly, the siRNA depletion of both Polk and FANCD2 simultaneously yielded similar levels of elevated SA-βgal activity and 53BP1 nuclear bodies as either of the individual siRNA depletions, suggesting that both of these proteins act within the same pathway (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mirin treatment to prevent nascent DNA degradation during HU pulse treatment does not alter the levels of 53BP1 nuclear bodies.
source: Significantly, mirin treatment to prevent nascent DNA degradation during the HU pulse treatment did not alter the levels of 53BP1 nuclear bodies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the replication-associated problems based on the loss of PolK and/or FANCD2 is caused by defects in fork restart efficiency, and not fork protection (MRE11-dependent nascent DNA degradation).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both PolK and the FA pathway cooperate within the same network that resolves replication stress from improperly stalled forks to help maintain genome integrity.
source: Thus, both PolK and the FA pathway cooperate within the same network that resolves replication stress from improperly stalled forks to help maintain genome integrity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence showing epistasis and similar phenotypes.

claim: Oncogene-induced DNA replication stress leads to activation of the DNA damage checkpoint, cell cycle arrest, senescence, and apoptosis.
source: One such barrier involves oncogene-induced DNA replication stress, which leads to activation of the DNA damage checkpoint, cell cycle arrest and/or senescence and apoptosis (Schoppy et al., 2012; Gilad et al., 2010; Murga et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Schoppy et al., 2012; Gilad et al., 2010; Murga et al., 2011).

claim: Early deregulation of the replication stress response could lead to sub-lethal genomic instability that becomes progressively worse in subsequent rounds of cell division.
source: We propose that early deregulation of the replication stress response could lead to sub-lethal genomic instability that becomes progressively worse in subsequent rounds of cell division as cells escape oncogene-induced senescence.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the consequences of replication stress response deregulation.

claim: A wide range of nucleotide starvation conditions, including oncogene-induced nucleotide exhaustion, could lead to dependence on PolK and/or the FA pathway.
source: Based on our studies, we predict that a wide range of nucleotide starvation conditions, including oncogene-induced nucleotide exhaustion, could lead to a dependence on PolK and/or the FA pathway to help mammalian cells withstand limited nucleotide availability via mechanisms involving fork restart.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation extrapolating from the experimental findings.

claim: PolK confers tolerance to oncogenic replication stress.
source: Interestingly, a recent study by Vaziri and colleagues showed that PolK confers tolerance to oncogenic replication stress (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: Under conditions of low dNTP levels, normal replicative polymerases are disfavored while TLS polymerases can readily engage at stalled replication forks.
source: Thus, we postulate that under certain conditions of low dNTP levels, the normal replicative polymerases (delta, epsilon) are disfavored in their usage while TLS Pols can readily engage at the stalled replication fork due to the low nucleotide concentration.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by the bacterial polymerase data cited earlier.

claim: Bacterial Y-family DNA polymerases Pol IV (DinB) and Pol V (UmuD2'C) enhance cell survival under conditions of nucleotide starvation.
source: This concept was originally proposed by Walker and colleagues, showing that the bacterial Y-family DNA polymerases Pol IV (DinB) and Pol V (UmuD2'C) enhance cell survival under conditions of nucleotide starvation (Godoy et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Godoy et al., 2006).

claim: PolK is intrinsically more processive and has higher fidelity than other Y-family TLS polymerases.
source: Additionally, PolK has been shown to be intrinsically more processive and has higher fidelity than the other Y-family TLS Pols (Lone et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Lone et al., 2007).

claim: Stabilization of the replisome by PolK during HU treatment provides fork protection against MRE11-dependent nuclease digestion and enables slower-moving forks as a temporary solution prior to normal DNA synthesis resumption.
source: The stabilization of the replisome by PolK during HU treatment provides at least two major advantages: 1) fork stalling events that lead to reversed fork structures would remain protected against MRE11-dependent nuclease digestion of nascent DNA, and 2) a moving fork (albeit slower-moving) provides a reasonable temporary solution or surrogate prior to the eventual resumption of normal DNA synthesis for fork restart after nucleotide levels rise again, leading to a more efficient fork recovery process (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and presented as a model in Figure 6D.

claim: Both PolH and PolK have been implicated in completing DNA replication at common fragile sites.
source: Previous studies have implicated both TLS Pol Eta (PolH) and PolK to complete DNA replication at common fragile sites (CFSs) (Barnes et al., 2017; Rey et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Barnes et al., 2017; Rey et al., 2009).

claim: Long poly(dA:dT) DNA tracts are preferred sites of replication fork stalling and collapse within early-replicating fragile sites and late-replicating common fragile sites.
source: Remarkably, they found that long poly(dA:dT) DNA tracts are preferred sites of replication fork stalling and collapse within early-replicating fragile sites (ERFSs) and late-replicating common fragile sites (CFSs).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work by Nussenzweig and colleagues (Tubbs et al., 2018).

claim: A PolK mutational signature has been discovered at fragile poly(dA:dT) DNA structures.
source: Intriguingly, they discovered a PolK mutational signature (Hile and Eckert, 2008) at these fragile poly(dA:dT) DNA structures, suggesting that throughout evolution, PolK has been employed during replication of these poly(dA:dT) repeats at these replication fork-stalling sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Tubbs et al., 2018; Hile and Eckert, 2008).

claim: The Fanconi Anemia pathway is activated via lysine site-specific monoubiquitination of FANCD2 and FANCI.
source: The FA pathway is activated via lysine site-specific monoubiquitination of two of its effector FA proteins, FANCD2 and FANCI (Garcia-Higuera et al., 2001; Sims et al., 2007; Smogorzewska et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Garcia-Higuera et al., 2001; Sims et al., 2007; Smogorzewska et al., 2007).

claim: The FA pathway is strongly activated by hydroxyurea (HU).
source: The FA pathway is strongly activated by hydroxyurea (HU) (Taniguchi et al., 2002), an inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase (RNR), which unlike ICL-inducing agents (such as mitomycin C or cisplatin), does not directly elicit DNA lesions that require removal, but induces severe replication fork slowing or stalling through the depletion of the cellular deoxynucleotide pool (dNTPs).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Taniguchi et al., 2002).

claim: FANCD2 and FANCI are associated with the replisome in response to replication fork arrest.
source: Additionally, recent studies found both FANCD2 and FANCI to be associated with the replisome in response to replication fork arrest and that the activation of the FA pathway is critical for protecting stalled forks from nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA during HU treatment, and for promoting fork restart after HU is removed (Lossaint et al., 2013; Schlacher et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lossaint et al., 2013; Schlacher et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).

claim: The activation of the FA pathway is critical for protecting stalled forks from nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA during HU treatment.
source: Additionally, recent studies found both FANCD2 and FANCI to be associated with the replisome in response to replication fork arrest and that the activation of the FA pathway is critical for protecting stalled forks from nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA during HU treatment, and for promoting fork restart after HU is removed (Lossaint et al., 2013; Schlacher et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lossaint et al., 2013; Schlacher et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).

claim: The activation of the FA pathway is critical for promoting fork restart after HU is removed.
source: Additionally, recent studies found both FANCD2 and FANCI to be associated with the replisome in response to replication fork arrest and that the activation of the FA pathway is critical for protecting stalled forks from nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA during HU treatment, and for promoting fork restart after HU is removed (Lossaint et al., 2013; Schlacher et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lossaint et al., 2013; Schlacher et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).

claim: The DNA damage tolerance (DDT) pathway is typically initiated by PCNA monoubiquitination and engagement of a specific Y-family TLS polymerase.
source: Specifically, the replication machinery can 'bypass' these physical barriers at stalled forks by swapping the replicative Pols for TLS Pols; this is known as the DNA damage tolerance (DDT) pathway that is typically initiated by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) monoubiquitination and engagement of a specific Y-family TLS Pol (such as Pol eta, kappa, iota, or Rev1) that possess ubiquitin-binding domains (UBDs) (Kannouche et al., 2004; Bienko et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kannouche et al., 2004; Bienko et al., 2005).

claim: Y-family TLS polymerases possess ubiquitin-binding domains (UBDs).
source: Specifically, the replication machinery can 'bypass' these physical barriers at stalled forks by swapping the replicative Pols for TLS Pols; this is known as the DNA damage tolerance (DDT) pathway that is typically initiated by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) monoubiquitination and engagement of a specific Y-family TLS Pol (such as Pol eta, kappa, iota, or Rev1) that possess ubiquitin-binding domains (UBDs) (Kannouche et al., 2004; Bienko et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kannouche et al., 2004; Bienko et al., 2005).

claim: The DDT pathway enables recruitment of TLS polymerases to bypass DNA lesions during or post S-phase DNA synthesis in the absence of repair.
source: The DDT pathway enables the recruitment of TLS Pols to bypass, or 'tolerate', the DNA lesions during or post S-phase DNA synthesis (in the absence of repair) in order to complete genome duplication in a timely manner and promote cell survival, but at a cost of increased mutagenesis (Sale et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Sale et al., 2012).

claim: Both the FA pathway and PCNA polyubiquitination are critical regulators of PolK recruitment and function at stalled forks.
source: Importantly, both the FA pathway and PCNA polyubiquitination are critical regulators of PolK recruitment and function at stalled forks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing PolK interaction with polyubiquitinated PCNA and epistasis with FA pathway.

claim: Fanconi Anemia is a chromosomal instability disorder caused by biallelic mutations in any of 21 FA genes.
source: The Fanconi Anemia (FA) disease is a chromosomal instability disorder that is caused by biallelic mutations in any of the 21 FA genes; FA is characterized by multiple developmental abnormalities, progressive bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition (Nalepa and Clapp, 2018; Ceccaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Nalepa and Clapp, 2018; Ceccaldi et al., 2016).

claim: Fanconi Anemia is characterized by multiple developmental abnormalities, progressive bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition.
source: The Fanconi Anemia (FA) disease is a chromosomal instability disorder that is caused by biallelic mutations in any of the 21 FA genes; FA is characterized by multiple developmental abnormalities, progressive bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition (Nalepa and Clapp, 2018; Ceccaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Nalepa and Clapp, 2018; Ceccaldi et al., 2016).

claim: The FA pathway plays a central role in the repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs).
source: The FA pathway, which includes FA gene products representing ubiquitin signaling, homology-directed recombination (HDR) and nucleolytic pathways, plays a central role in the repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs) and regulates cellular responses to replication stress (Kottemann and Smogorzewska, 2013; Michl et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kottemann and Smogorzewska, 2013; Michl et al., 2016a).

claim: The FA pathway regulates cellular responses to replication stress.
source: The FA pathway, which includes FA gene products representing ubiquitin signaling, homology-directed recombination (HDR) and nucleolytic pathways, plays a central role in the repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs) and regulates cellular responses to replication stress (Kottemann and Smogorzewska, 2013; Michl et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kottemann and Smogorzewska, 2013; Michl et al., 2016a).

claim: Replication stress in dividing cells often leads to increased stalled forks and under-replication of DNA.
source: Replication stress in dividing cells often leads to increased stalled forks and under-replication of the DNA, which can ultimately contribute to elevated DNA damage, mutagenesis and genomic instability (Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).

claim: One of the most common human diseases associated with replication stress is cancer.
source: One of the most common human diseases associated with replication stress is cancer (Bartek et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Bartek et al., 2012).

claim: PolK was previously shown to be important for facilitating Chk1 phosphorylation in response to replication stress.
source: A previous study showed that PolK was important for facilitating Chk1 phosphorylation in response to replication stress (Bétous et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Bétous et al., 2013).

claim: FANCD2 is necessary for actively restraining DNA synthesis upon nucleotide deprivation.
source: Previous studies showed that FANCD2 is necessary for actively restraining DNA synthesis upon nucleotide deprivation (Lossaint et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Michl et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lossaint et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Michl et al., 2016b).

claim: In FANCD2-depleted cells, faster fork speed in the presence of HU is largely dependent on PolK.
source: In FANCD2-depleted cells, the faster fork speed (longer CldU tracts) in the presence of HU is largely dependent on PolK (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The phenotype in PolK-deficient mice in the absence of perturbations is relatively mild.
source: Despite significant defects in replication fork protection and fork restart in response to HU treatment, the phenotype in PolK-deficient mice in the absence of perturbations is relatively mild (Burr et al., 2006; Stancel et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Burr et al., 2006; Stancel et al., 2009).

claim: Asynchronous growing PolK-deficient cells have normal cell cycle progression compared to control cells.
source: Asynchronous growing PolK-deficient cells have a normal cell cycle progression in comparison to control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PolK-deficient cells do not experience higher levels of DNA damage or cell cycle checkpoint activation in response to HU and HU wash off.
source: They also do not experience higher levels of DNA damage or cell cycle checkpoint activation in response to HU and HU wash off (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A, 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.
